lessons.culture: In Cairo "الحمد لله" is the automatic answer to "إزيك؟" whatever your mood, and a close friend who senses something off will follow with "مالك؟". Saying "زعلان" or "تعبان" outright is normal only with people you trust.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "إزيك النهارده؟". Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but bookish; "الحمد لله" is the natural spoken answer.

exercises.tip: "الحمد لله" is added almost automatically after saying you're fine.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "مالك، شكلك تعبان؟". Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: Formal written Arabic, not how tiredness is admitted in conversation.

exercises.tip: "شوية" softens the admission, like "a little".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أنا ___ أوي، عايز آكل حاجة." Meaning: I'm very hungry, I want to eat something.

too_formal.feedback: Formal way of stating hunger; "جعان" is the word actually used.

exercises.tip: "جعان" for a man, "جعانة" for a woman. Cairenes say ج as g: ga3aan.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أنا ___ من ده." Meaning: I'm scared of this.

too_formal.feedback: Formal spelling and register; "خايف" is how it's said out loud.

exercises.tip: "خايف" for a man, "خايفة" for a woman.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'm very happy today."

too_formal.feedback: "سعيد" is the formal word for happy; Cairenes say "مبسوط", and "أوي" for very.

exercises.tip: "أوي" is the everyday Egyptian "very", not "جداً".

too_formal.feedback: Overly formal phrasing for a simple everyday worry.

exercises.tip: In Cairo ق is a glottal stop: 2al2aan.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "I'm worried"?

too_formal.feedback: Nobody speaks like this out loud; it belongs in writing.

exercises.tip: "قلقان" comes from the same root as "قلق", worry.

too_formal.feedback: A dictionary-style gloss, not the plain answer expected here.

exercises.tip: "زعلان" is milder than "angry"; closer to "upset" or "put out".

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "أوي / النهارده / مبسوط / أنا".

too_formal.feedback: Formal register and word order, not the conversational sentence being practised.

exercises.tip: Subject first, then the feeling, then how much, then when.

too_formal.feedback: Formal wording, not what is said in conversation.

exercises.tip: "من" follows "خايف" to name what you fear.

lessons.culture: Egyptians disagree warmly and often with humour; "عندك حق" and "بالظبط" keep a talk friendly, while a soft "جايز، بس..." is the usual way to push back on an elder or a boss. A flat "لا" with no softener can sound blunt.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "الأكل هنا حلو أوي، مش كده؟". Agree naturally.

too_formal.feedback: Formal and stiff; "بالظبط" is the natural spoken agreement.

exercises.tip: "بالظبط" is the usual way to say "exactly".

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "أنا شايف إننا نروح بكره.". Say maybe, but you're busy.

too_formal.feedback: Bookish; "جايز، بس" is how Cairenes soften a refusal.

exercises.tip: "جايز" means "maybe, it's possible".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أنا ___ معاك." Meaning: I agree with you. (m)

too_formal.feedback: Formal; "موافق معاك" is what's said.

exercises.tip: "موافقة" if a woman is speaking. "أنا معاك" is just as common.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "ده ___ صح." Meaning: That's not right.

too_formal.feedback: "غير" is written Arabic; Cairenes use "مش" before nearly everything.

exercises.tip: "مش" is the everyday negation before nouns and adjectives.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I don't agree with you."

too_formal.feedback: The formal written way of disagreeing.

exercises.tip: A woman says "مش موافقة".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "OK, that works."

too_formal.feedback: Overly formal for accepting a plan.

exercises.tip: "ماشي" means "fine, deal".

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "I agree" said by a woman?

too_formal.feedback: Formal, and does not mark gender the way the spoken form does.

exercises.tip: "موافقة" ends in ة for a woman speaking; "موافق" is for a man.

exercises.prompt: "ده مش صح" means:

too_formal.feedback: A formal restatement, not the plain meaning asked for.

exercises.tip: "مش" is the everyday negation.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "حق / عندك".

too_formal.feedback: "أنت على حق" is formal; "عندك حق" is what's actually said.

exercises.tip: "معاك حق" is just as common.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "الجديد / المطعم / نروح / في رأيي".

lessons.culture: In Egypt advice is given freely and warmly, even by strangers, usually wrapped in "لازم" or "أحسن", and the sick are met with "ألف سلامة". Answering "حاضر" is the polite way to take advice.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "أنا تعبان أوي النهارده.". Give friendly advice.

too_formal.feedback: Sounds like a textbook; "لازم" is the spoken "you should".

exercises.tip: "لازم" is stronger than "أحسن", closer to "you really should".

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "أعمل إيه في الصداع ده؟". Suggest the medicine.

exercises.tip: Egyptians say "دوا" with no hamza.

lessons.culture: In Cairo a complaint lands best after "لو سمحت" and a smile, and staff answer with "خير يا فندم؟" and "معلش" for a delay. Raising your voice is more likely to start an argument than to fix the bill.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but written-style; "فيه" is the spoken "there is".

exercises.tip: "فيه" means "there is"; "مفيش" means "there isn't".

exercises.tip: "ولا يهمك" literally means "it shouldn't concern you".

lessons.culture: Egyptians thank generously: متشكر for small things, تسلم إيدك (bless your hand) for food or help, and عمري ما هنسى جميلك for a big favour. جزاك الله خيرًا, answered وإياك, is said exactly the same in every dialect; مبروك is answered الله يبارك فيك, and ما شاء الله comes first when praising someone.

exercises.prompt: A man says to you: "جزاك الله خيرًا". Reply.
exercises.tip: This formula is shared by all dialects; to a woman: وإياكِ.

exercises.prompt: A friend says to you: "مبروك!". Reply (to a man).

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but the expected answer to مبروك is a du'a: الله يبارك فيك.

exercises.tip: To a woman: الله يبارك فيكي.

too_formal.feedback: Written Arabic; Egyptians say "عمري ما هنسى".

exercises.tip: "جميل" here means a favour you owe someone.

lessons.culture: Egyptians soften an apology with معلش and settle it with حصل خير (no harm done) or ولا يهمك; a broken glass is often waved off with فداك, "it was worth less than you". The written du'a غفر الله لنا ولكم is the same in every dialect, while in everyday speech Cairenes say ربنا يغفرلنا.

too_formal.feedback: Understood, but "لا بأس" is formal in Cairo; people say "معلش" or "حصل خير".

exercises.tip: "حصل خير" = literally "good happened", i.e. no harm done.

too_formal.feedback: Understood, but Egyptians use the participle: "مسامحك".

exercises.tip: A woman says مسامحاك.

exercises.tip: "غلطة" = mistake; "غلطتي" = my mistake.

exercises.tip: A man says أنا آسف.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Egyptian: "Don't be sad, it happens to everyone." (to a man)
exercises.answer: مَا تِزْعَلْش، دِي بِتِحْصَل لِكُلّ النَّاس
accepted: مَا تِزْعَلْش، دِي بِتِحْصَل لِكُلّ النَّاس
ما تزعلش، دي بتحصل لكل الناس
ma tez3alsh, dee bte7Sal le-koll en-naas

too_formal.feedback: Written Arabic; Egyptians say "ما تزعلش".

exercises.tip: To a woman: ما تزعليش.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "I apologize for being late"?

too_formal.feedback: Written Arabic; Egyptians say "بعتذر على التأخير".

exercises.tip: Present tense in Egyptian takes بـ: بعتذر.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "No harm done, it is a small matter"?
exercises.tip: "ولا يهمك" = don't worry about it.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: "الجاية / بالي / هاخد / المرة / أكتر"

too_formal.item: سأكون أكثر حذرًا في المرة القادمة
too_formal.feedback: Written Arabic; Egyptians say "هاخد بالي" and "الجاية".

exercises.tip: "المرة الجاية" = next time.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: "كلنا / ربنا / يغفرلنا"

too_formal.feedback: Correct and shared by all dialects as a written du'a; in Cairo speech it is "ربنا يغفرلنا كلنا".

exercises.tip: "ربنا" is how Egyptians usually say Allah in everyday du'a.

challenge.title: How Was Your Week?
challenge.instructions: Write a short conversation between two friends who run into each other. One asks how the other is feeling, hears about a problem, gives some advice, and the other politely raises one more small complaint before agreeing on what to do.
required_elements: a question asking how someone feels, using "إزيك" or "إزيّك"
at least one feeling word such as "تعبان", "مبسوط" or "قلقان"
a piece of advice using "لازم" or "أحسن"
agreement or disagreement using "عندك حق" or "مش موافق"
a polite complaint opened with "لو سمحت" or "آسف على الإزعاج"

dialogue.speaker: Hala
dialogue.english: How are you today?

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.arabic: أنا قلقان شوية، عندي شغل كتير
dialogue.english: I'm a little worried, I have a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Hala
dialogue.arabic: أحسن تاخد شوية راحة قبل ما تتعب أكتر
dialogue.transliteration: a7san taakhod shwayyet raa7a 2abl ma tit3ab aktar
dialogue.english: It's better you get some rest before you get more tired.

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.english: Maybe you're right.

dialogue.speaker: Hala
dialogue.transliteration: w khod baalak min nafsak ba2a
dialogue.english: And take care of yourself, then.

dialogue.speaker: Omar
dialogue.arabic: تمام، شكراً. آسف على الإزعاج، بس المكان ده زحمة أوي، نمشي؟
dialogue.transliteration: tamaam, shukran. aasef 3al-ez3aag, bas el-makaan da zo7ma awi, nemshi?
dialogue.english: OK, thanks. Sorry to bother you, but this place is very crowded, shall we go?
